cse-2015-1-cs-42.approach: For a single-entry single-exit program, cyclomatic complexity = number of binary decision points + 1.

steps.title: Count the predicates
steps.body:
1. `while (first <= last)`
2. `if (array[middle] < search)`
3. `else if (array[middle] == search)`
4. `if (first > last)`

That is $P = 4$ binary decisions.

pitfalls: Counting the final `else` as a separate decision — it is the false branch of the `else if`.
cse-2015-1-cs-42.verification: Regions of the planar CFG: the while loop, the if, the else-if and the final if each add one bounded region, plus the outer region = 5; equivalently $E - N + 2$ on the drawn CFG gives 5.

cse-2015-1-cs-43.approach: Use the cycle property: each non-MST edge must be heavier than every MST edge on the tree path between its endpoints. Give each non-MST edge the smallest unused integer above that maximum.

steps.title: Non-MST edges
steps.body: The 8 edges are A–B, A–C, B–C, B–E, C–D, D–E, E–F, D–F. The non-MST ones are **A–B, C–D, D–E**.

steps.title: A–B
steps.body: Tree path A–C–B has max weight $\max(9,2)=9$. So $w(AB) > 9$; smallest distinct integer is **10**.

steps.title: C–D
steps.body: Tree path C–B–E–F–D has weights 2, 15, 4, 6; max = 15. So $w(CD) > 15$ ⇒ **16**.

steps.title: D–E
steps.body: Tree path D–F–E has max $\max(6,4)=6$. So $w(DE) > 6$; 7 is unused ⇒ **7**.

pitfalls: Using only the edge's own triangle for C–D: its tree path goes through B–E (15), so it must exceed 15.
Reusing an existing weight (weights are distinct).
cse-2015-1-cs-43.verification: 10, 16, 7 are all distinct from {2, 4, 6, 9, 15}, and each is the smallest value making the given tree the unique MST.

cse-2015-1-cs-44.approach: The integrand is $\cos(u)$ times the derivative of $u = 1/x$ (up to sign), so substitute $u = 1/x$.

steps.title: Substitute
steps.body:
$u = 1/x \Rightarrow du = -\dfrac{dx}{x^2}$. Limits: $x = 1/\pi \to u = \pi$, $x = 2/\pi \to u = \pi/2$.
$$I = \int_{\pi}^{\pi/2} -\cos u\,du = \int_{\pi/2}^{\pi} \cos u\,du$$

steps.title: Evaluate
steps.body: $$I = \sin\pi - \sin\tfrac{\pi}{2} = 0 - 1 = -1$$

pitfalls: Dropping the minus sign from $du$ (gives +1).

cse-2015-1-cs-45.approach: In BFS on an undirected graph, the endpoints of any edge have distances differing by at most 1 (otherwise the farther one would have been discovered earlier through this edge).

steps.title: Edge property
steps.body: For any edge $(u,v)$: $d(v) \le d(u) + 1$ and $d(u) \le d(v) + 1$, so $|d(u) - d(v)| \le 1$.

steps.title: Non-tree edges
steps.body: A non-tree edge can join two vertices on the same level ($0$) or adjacent levels ($\pm1$). A difference of $2$ is impossible for any edge, tree or not. Option (D).

optionAnalysis.reason: Possible: e.g. s–a, s–b, a–c, b–c; the non-tree edge (b, c) has $d(b) - d(c) = 1 - 2 = -1$.
Possible: an edge between two vertices on the same level (a triangle s, a, b gives non-tree edge a–b).
Possible: same example as (A) read as (c, b): $2 - 1 = 1$.
Endpoints of any edge differ by at most one level.

cse-2015-1-cs-45.verification: If $d(u) = d(v) + 2$, then path to $v$ plus edge $(v,u)$ gives $d(u) \le d(v)+1$, a contradiction.

cse-2015-1-cs-46.approach: Rate-monotonic priorities: T1 (period 3) > T2 (period 7) > T3 (period 20). Simulate the pre-emptive schedule millisecond by millisecond until T3 has received 4 ms.
cse-2015-1-cs-46.given:
| Task | Period | Execution | Priority |
|---|---|---|---|
| $T_1$ | 3 | 1 | highest |
| $T_2$ | 7 | 2 | middle |
| $T_3$ | 20 | 4 | lowest |

steps.title: 0 – 3 ms
steps.body: All arrive at 0. $T_1$ runs 0–1 (done), $T_2$ runs 1–3 (done).

scene.caption: T1 then T2; T3 still waiting.

steps.title: 3 – 7 ms
steps.body: $T_1$ (2nd job, arrived 3) runs 3–4. $T_3$ runs 4–6 (2 of 4 ms done). $T_1$ (3rd job, arrived 6) pre-empts and runs 6–7.

scene.caption: T3 has 2 ms done by t = 6.

steps.title: 7 – 10 ms
steps.body: $T_2$ (2nd job, arrived 7) runs 7–9. $T_1$ (4th job, arrived 9) runs 9–10.

steps.title: 10 – 12 ms
steps.body:
No other job is ready until $T_1$'s next arrival at 12, so $T_3$ runs 10–12 and finishes its remaining 2 ms.

It completes at the **end of the 12th millisecond**.

pitfalls: Forgetting that T1's job at t = 6 pre-empts T3.
Giving T2 its second job at t = 6 instead of t = 7.
cse-2015-1-cs-46.verification: In [0,12): T1 uses 4 jobs × 1 = 4 ms, T2 uses 2 × 2 = 4 ms, T3 uses 4 ms; 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 with no idle time.

cse-2015-1-cs-47.approach: Simulate both policies with 5 frames on the 15 references and count faults.

steps.title: Cold start
steps.body: References 3, 8, 2, 3, 9, 1: pages 3, 8, 2, 9, 1 fault (5 faults), the second 3 hits. All 5 frames are now full — same for both policies.

steps.title: FIFO
steps.body:
Queue (oldest first) 3, 8, 2, 9, 1.
- 6: fault, evict 3 → 8, 2, 9, 1, 6
- 3: fault, evict 8 → 2, 9, 1, 6, 3
- 8: fault, evict 2 → 9, 1, 6, 3, 8
- 9, 3, 6: hits
- 2: fault, evict 9 → 1, 6, 3, 8, 2
- 1, 3: hits

FIFO faults $= 5 + 4 = 9$.

steps.title: LRU
steps.body:
Recency (least recent first) after cold start: 8, 2, 3, 9, 1.
- 6: fault, evict 8 → 2, 3, 9, 1, 6
- 3: hit → 2, 9, 1, 6, 3
- 8: fault, evict 2 → 9, 1, 6, 3, 8
- 9, 3, 6: hits → 1, 8, 9, 3, 6
- 2: fault, evict 1 → 8, 9, 3, 6, 2
- 1: fault, evict 8 → 9, 3, 6, 2, 1
- 3: hit

LRU faults $= 5 + 4 = 9$.

steps.title: Compare
steps.body: FIFO = 9, LRU = 9 ⇒ both incur the same number of faults: option (A).

answer.value: Both incur the same number of page faults

optionAnalysis.reason: Both policies give 9 faults.
FIFO is not 2 more; the counts are equal (9 each).
LRU is not 2 more; the counts are equal.
The difference is 0, not 1.

pitfalls: Updating FIFO order on a hit — FIFO order changes only on loads.
Forgetting that the repeated 3 at position 4 is a hit during the cold start.
cse-2015-1-cs-47.verification: The paging simulator reproduces 9 faults for both FIFO and LRU with 5 frames.

cse-2015-1-cs-48.approach: Each sector costs one seek + average rotational latency + one-sector transfer time; multiply by the number of sectors.

steps.title: Rotation-based times
steps.body:
10000 RPM ⇒ one rotation $= \dfrac{60{,}000 \text{ ms}}{10000} = 6$ ms.
- Average latency $= 6/2 = 3$ ms
- Transfer of one sector $= 6/600 = 0.01$ ms

pitfalls: Dropping the 0.01 ms transfer time (gives 14000).
Using a full rotation as latency (gives 20020).

cse-2015-1-cs-49.approach: Split strings of length n by how they start: 0…, 10…, 11…. Each case reduces to a smaller problem or is already satisfied.

steps.title: Starts with 0
steps.body: The remaining $n-1$ bits must contain "11": $a_{n-1}$ strings.

steps.title: Starts with 10
steps.body: The leading "10" cannot help form "11", so the remaining $n-2$ bits must contain it: $a_{n-2}$ strings.

steps.title: Starts with 11
steps.body:
Already contains "11"; the other $n-2$ bits are free: $2^{n-2}$ strings.

$$a_n = a_{n-1} + a_{n-2} + 2^{n-2}$$ — option (A).

optionAnalysis.reason: Exactly the three-case split 0…, 10…, 11….
$2a_{n-1}$ double counts; the first-bit-1 case is not equivalent to a length $n-1$ problem.
$2a_{n-2}$ would count the 11… prefix twice (it is already in $2^{n-2}$).
Both coefficients overcount.

cse-2015-1-cs-50.approach: Run backward liveness on the 4-block CFG: $\text{in}(B) = \text{use}(B) \cup (\text{out}(B) - \text{def}(B))$, $\text{out}(B) = \bigcup \text{in}(\text{succ})$. Blocks 2 and 3 have a single statement, so 'live at the statement' is live-in of the block.
cse-2015-1-cs-50.given:
| Block | Code | use (before def) | def | succ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | p=q+r; s=p+q; u=s*v | q, r, v | p, s, u | 2, 3 |
| 2 | v=r+u | r, u | v | 4 |
| 3 | q=s*u | s, u | q | 4 |
| 4 | q=v+r | v, r | q | 1 |

steps.title: Block 1 and 4
steps.body:
$\text{in}(1) = \{q, r, v\}$ (q and r used in `p=q+r`, v used in `u=s*v`, none defined earlier in the block; p, s, u are defined before use).

$\text{out}(4) = \text{in}(1) = \{q, r, v\}$, so
$$\text{in}(4) = \{v, r\} \cup (\{q,r,v\} - \{q\}) = \{r, v\}$$

steps.title: Intersection
steps.body: $$\{r,u\} \cap \{r,s,u,v\} = \{r, u\}$$ — option (C).

optionAnalysis.reason: p is defined in block 1 before any use, so it is dead at blocks 2 and 3; s is not live at block 2.
s is live at block 3 (used there) but not at block 2 — nothing reachable from block 2 uses s before block 1 redefines it.
r and u are live at both statements.
q is redefined in block 4 before reaching any use; v is assigned at block 2's own statement, so it is not live there.

pitfalls: Counting v as live at block 2 — condition iii excludes an assignment at $S_i$ itself.
Following the back edge to block 1 and forgetting q is redefined in block 4 first.
cse-2015-1-cs-50.verification: Iterating the equations a second time leaves every set unchanged (fixed point).

cse-2015-1-cs-51.approach: In $q_0$ the PDA pushes every symbol; it guesses the middle (optionally consuming one symbol) and moves to $q_1$, where each input must be the complement of the stack top. So it accepts $w\,c\,\overline{w}^R$ with $c \in \{0,1,\varepsilon\}$, where $\overline{w}^R$ is the reversed complement of $w$.

steps.title: Language
steps.body:
- $q_0$: read $0$/$1$, push it.
- $q_0 \to q_1$: read one symbol or nothing, stack unchanged (the middle).
- $q_1$: read 0 only if top is 1, read 1 only if top is 0; pop.
- $q_1 \to q_2$ on $\bot$.

Accepted: $w\,c\,\overline{w}^{R}$, $|c| \le 1$.

steps.title: Locate the middle
steps.body: Every option has length 5, so the full string has $6 + 5 = 11$ symbols (odd). Hence $c$ is one symbol and $|w| = 5$: $w = 10110$, $c = 0$ (6th symbol).

steps.title: Required suffix
steps.body: $\overline{w} = 01001$; reversed: $\overline{w}^R = 10010$. Option (B).

optionAnalysis.reason: 10110 is $w$ itself, not its reversed complement: the first two symbols pop fine (1 on top 0, 0 on top 1), but the third symbol 1 meets top 1 → stuck.
Exactly the reversed complement of 10110.
01010: first symbol 0 needs top 1, but top is 0 (last pushed symbol of $w$) → stuck.
01001 is the complement without reversal; the first 0 meets top 0 → stuck.

cse-2015-1-cs-51.verification: Stack after pushing 10110 (top last): 1,0,1,1,0. Reading 1,0,0,1,0 pops 0,1,1,0,1 — each a complement match — leaving ⊥, then ε-move to $q_2$.

cse-2015-1-cs-52.approach: Identify each language from its diagram: M accepts exactly the strings ending in a, N exactly those ending in b. No string ends in both, so the intersection is empty.
concepts: Minimal DFA of the empty language

steps.title: L(M) and L(N)
steps.body: In M every a leads to the accepting state and every b to the start state, so $L(M) = \{x : x \text{ ends in } a\}$. Symmetrically $L(N) = \{x : x \text{ ends in } b\}$. Neither contains $\varepsilon$.

steps.title: Intersection
steps.body: A string cannot end in both a and b, so $L(M) \cap L(N) = \varnothing$. The minimal DFA for $\varnothing$ is a single non-accepting state looping on a, b: **1** state.

pitfalls: Building the 4-state product DFA and not minimising it.
Answering 0 — a (complete) DFA needs at least the start state.
cse-2015-1-cs-52.verification: In the product automaton the only accepting pair (M-accept, N-accept) is unreachable, so all reachable states are non-accepting and merge into one.

cse-2015-1-cs-53.approach: Stop-and-wait utilisation is $U = \dfrac{T_t}{T_t + 2T_p}$. Set $U \ge 0.5$, solve for $T_t$, convert to bits and bytes.

steps.title: Condition
steps.body: $$\frac{T_t}{T_t + 2T_p} \ge \frac12 \;\Rightarrow\; T_t \ge 2T_p = 2 \times 20 = 40 \text{ ms}$$

steps.title: Frame size
steps.body: $$L = T_t \times B = 0.04 \times 64000 = 2560 \text{ bits} = \frac{2560}{8} = 320 \text{ bytes}$$

pitfalls: Using one-way delay (gives 160 bytes).
Taking 64 kb as 65536 bits — link rates use 1 k = 1000.

cse-2015-1-cs-54.approach: Every face is a triangle, so counting face–edge incidences gives $3F = 2E$; combine with Euler's formula $V - E + F = 2$.

steps.title: Face count
steps.body: Each edge borders 2 faces and each face has 3 edges: $3F = 2E \Rightarrow F = \tfrac{2E}{3}$.

steps.title: Euler
steps.body: $$10 - E + \frac{2E}{3} = 2 \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{E}{3} = 8 \;\Rightarrow\; E = 24$$

pitfalls: Forgetting the outer face, which is also a triangle here.
cse-2015-1-cs-54.verification: Maximal planar bound $3V - 6 = 24$ — a triangulation attains it exactly; $F = 16$, and $10 - 24 + 16 = 2$ ✓.

cse-2015-1-cs-55.approach: In SSA every assignment creates a new name, so no temporary can be reused. Generate three-address code with one operator per instruction and count the temporaries.

steps.title: Order of evaluation
steps.body:
With precedence and left-to-right associativity:
$$((((q + r/3) + s) - t*5) + (u*v)/w)$$
There are 8 operators: /, +, +, *, −, *, /, +.

steps.title: Three-address code
steps.body:
```
t1 = r / 3
t2 = q + t1
t3 = t2 + s
t4 = t * 5
t5 = t3 - t4
t6 = u * v
t7 = t6 / w
t8 = t5 + t7
```
Each instruction defines a fresh name (SSA forbids reusing one), so **8** temporaries.

pitfalls: Reusing a temporary (e.g. `t1 = t1 + s`) — legal in ordinary TAC, illegal in SSA.
Counting only 7 by storing the final result directly into a program variable — the expression has no target variable.
cse-2015-1-cs-55.verification: One new name per binary operator: 8 operators ⇒ 8 temporaries.
